# Ten Example Levels

Ten levels, ten structural motifs, ten different palettes. Regenerate the whole set with:

```bash
python3 content-data/maps/make-example-levels.py   # maps, validated before writing
python3 content-data/maps/render-atlas.py          # top-down schematic, no display needed
python3 content-data/maps/capture-iso-atlas.py     # real frames from the editor, needs a display
```

**All ten now pass the validator and all three `MapTargets` bands** — three of them did not when this
document first claimed they did; see below. Three new themes — `tundra`, `ash`, `marsh` — were added
so every level gets its own palette; their tiles were generated automatically from the ramp, since the
tile script reads the registry.

**Five of ten motifs survive the projection.** The generator lays out a shape on a top-down grid, and
the schematic atlas showed that shape faithfully — but the game is drawn at the iso angle, where a
wall is a solid block with height and everything behind it is hidden. `comb`, `ringfort`, `atoll` and
`switchback` are legible as the thing they are named after. `spiral`, `chambers`, `braid` and
`stepwell` are not, and no amount of balancing will make a player see a braid in `braid`.

## They are NOT balanced, and the spread is the finding

Wave tables are copied from `crossroads` and not re-tuned. All ten at 150 runs:

| Level | Runs lost | Lives left | sd | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `comb` | 42.0% | 7.0 | 5.9 | above band |
| `spiral` | **25.3%** | 7.7 | 6.7 | **in band** — the only one, and by accident; see below |
| `chambers` | 0.7% | 11.8 | 5.7 | too easy |
| `braid` | 0.7% | 18.6 | 2.9 | too easy |
| `switchback` | 0.0% | 16.9 | 4.1 | too easy |
| `atoll` | 0.0% | 17.9 | 4.1 | too easy |
| `ringfort` | 0.0% | 19.9 | 0.2 | degenerate |
| `meander` | 0.0% | 20.0 | 0.0 | degenerate |
| `stepwell` | 0.0% | 20.0 | 0.0 | degenerate |
| `driftway` | 0.0% | 19.7 | 0.4 | degenerate |

**Ten maps, every one inside every `MapTargets` band, outcomes from 0% to 42%.**

That is the result worth keeping. The bands are a **legality and shape check, not a difficulty check**,
and nothing in them predicts how a map plays. Any new map needs a balance pass; the report cannot
stand in for one.

### `spiral` was unwinnable, and the cause is corridor width

It lost **100% of 150 runs** — every life, every time, sd 0.0 — while passing every band.

The cause is not area, it is **width**. Its route ran down a **one-cell canyon**, so a tower could
only reach the route from exactly two cells away, at the very limit of arrow range. Each tower
covered a sliver: **six towers stopped 12% of wave 1, where the same six stop 100% on `meander`.**

Widening the corridors to two cells fixed it outright — 100% → **41.3% lost, sd 7.6**, a hard level
with real variance instead of a wall.

> **A one-cell-wide route is not a hard level, it is an undefendable one.** Range is measured from
> cell centres, so a corridor narrower than the tower's reach leaves nowhere to stand. Nothing in
> `MapTargets` sees this, and neither `cover` nor `useful` predicted it — both read normal on
> `spiral` while it was losing every run.

The generator now emits two-wide corridors, and refuses any map under 50% `useful`.

### Then five dead cells moved it another 16 points

Sealing `spiral`'s five walled-off cells (above) was filed as tidying. It was not. Same seed, same 150
runs, the map's only change being those five cells painted blocked:

| `spiral` | Runs lost | Lives left | sd | `useful` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| with 5 stranded cells | 41.3% | 8.4 | 7.6 | 60% |
| sealed | **25.3%** | 7.7 | 6.7 | 64% |

**A walled-off buildable cell is a decoy, not a blemish.** The scripted policy builds on it, the tower
never fires, and the run is down a tower it paid for. Five cells out of seventy-three were worth
sixteen points of run-loss — enough to carry the map from above the 15–30% band into it. A player
reads the same board and makes the same mistake, with no warning that the plot they just bought is dead.

This sharpens the `useful` finding rather than overturning it. Earlier, raising `spiral`'s `useful`
from 43% to 60% **by adding cells near the route** changed its outcome not at all. Here, raising it
from 60% to 64% **by deleting cells far from it** moved the map 16 points. The metric was never wrong
about which cells matter — it was being read as a dial to turn up, when what mattered was the count of
cells that actively mislead. Whether that generalises is untested: `stepwell` (6 sealed) and `driftway`
(2 sealed) did not budge, both being degenerate for other reasons.

### Two candidates ruled out on the way

Recorded so nobody spends the evening again:

- **Maze multiplier** (`maze` column, the editor's F6 estimate) does not measure route variance.
  `gauntlet` is 1.0× and `crossroads` 1.1× — adjacent — while their outcome spread is sd 0.0 against
  sd 7.1. A threshold at 1.15× flagged nine of twelve maps including a known-good one. The column is
  kept as information; the warning was removed.
- **Buildable-share-of-route** does not either. `gauntlet` is 96% buildable-on-route, the same as
  every other map, so "can you build on the path" separates nothing.

`ringfort` still reproduces `gauntlet`'s signature — 0.0% lost, sd 0.2 — and both remain unexplained by
any metric here. That is still open: `route-variance-metric`.

## How the generator satisfies bands that fight each other

`MapTargets` wants buildable at 35–55% **and** path 18–30, and the map report proposes density ≤ 2.0.
On a large grid those cannot all hold: at 20×9, 40% buildable is 72 cells against a route capped at
30, so density is 2.4 before anything else happens — and `crossroads` sits at 4.0.

Hence small grids (~13×12) with routes near the top of the band. Even then the last two bands pull
opposite ways, because a longer route needs more scenery and more scenery eats the buildable floor.
The generator's `thin()` runs two passes: the first keeps a block **only if it bends the route**,
buying length at the lowest cost in buildable; the second fills in anywhere, and neither may cross
37%.

Blind blocking was tried first and dropped six of ten maps to 26–34% buildable.

## What the first in-engine look found

All twelve maps were captured in the editor on 2026-08-08 and looked at — the check this document
listed as outstanding. Three things came out of it.

### Three maps were shipping validator warnings

`spiral`, `stepwell` and `driftway` each carried a `MapValidator` warning — **5, 6 and 2 buildable
cells walled off and unable to ever matter** — while this document said all ten passed. Nobody was
lying: nothing anyone ran was showing it.

The cause is that `make-example-levels.py` **re-implemented the validator instead of calling it**. Its
`problems` list checked reachability, path band, buildable band, spawn-goal distance and `useful` — and
not stranded cells, which is a check `MapValidator` does make. So the generator passed its own weaker
exam and printed `ok`, and the only thing that would have disagreed was the editor, which nobody could
run. `Gridfall.Verify -- maps` did not catch it either: **it reports geometry and never calls
`MapValidator` at all.**

This is precisely what the board editor's own header warns against — *"it contributes no rules of its
own, so it cannot disagree with the game about what a legal map is"*. The generator did contribute its
own rules, and lost.

Fixed by `seal_strays()`: after thinning, a walled-off buildable cell is painted blocked, which is what
it already was in every respect but the map's own account of itself. A backstop `problems` entry now
refuses to write a map if any survive. Only the three affected maps changed; `spiral` 43→40% buildable,
`stepwell` 52→49%, `driftway` 52→51%, all still inside the 35–55% band, and `useful` rose on all three.

> **A generator that validates its own output is only as good as the copy of the rules it carries.**
> The next one should shell out to the real validator, not paraphrase it.

### The motif is a top-down claim, and the game is not top-down

See the `Reads at iso` column. The schematic atlas is honest about cell layout and says nothing about
legibility, because it draws no walls, no height and no occlusion. Four of the ten motifs disappear
at the projection the player actually uses.

Worth noting but **not yet a rule**: the two boards whose geometry does the most visible work — `comb`
(2.1× floor) and `crossroads` (the only tuned board) — are also the two with real outcome variance,
while `chambers`, `braid` and `stepwell` are all both illegible and too easy. `ringfort` and `atoll`
break it: both read well and both are degenerate. So legibility is not the missing metric either.

### Only two of twelve maps have road terrain

`crossroads` has 42 `PathOnly` cells and `ringfort` 32. **The other ten have none** — they are binary
buildable/blocked, so the route exists only in the flow field and is drawn only by the editor's route
overlay. In the game there is no overlay, which means on eight of these boards a player cannot see
where the creeps will walk until they walk. `crossroads` reads as a place with roads through it; the
generated boards read as a field with a dotted line over it. The generator never emits `PathOnly`.

## Palettes: the three new ones are fine, the set is crowded

`ash`, `marsh` and `tundra` all render correctly and all 75 tiles are present. Perceptual distance
(CIE76 ΔE on the buildable ground colour, from `TerrainTheme.cs`) between every pair of themes, worst
first:

| Pair | ΔE buildable | |
|---|---|---|
| `ocean` / `slate` | 8.6 | pre-existing |
| `slate` / `tundra` | 9.9 | **new** |
| `ash` / `mountain` | 10.2 | **new** |
| `space` / `underwater` | 10.4 | pre-existing |
| `ash` / `marsh` | 10.6 | **new** |

The new palettes are **no worse than the seven already shipped** — the tightest pair in the set is
`ocean`/`slate`, which predates them. But every pair under ΔE 11 is a pair of desaturated blue-greys,
and the set now has six of them. On the contact sheet the one to watch is `atoll` (tundra) against
`switchback` and `crossroads` (slate): at thumbnail size they read as the same material.

ΔE on the flat colour is a lower bound on confusion, not a verdict — tile noise and lighting add
separation the number cannot see. The contact sheet is the evidence; the table only says where to look.

## Known Not Verified

- **Motion, feel and taste.** Frames are captured; nobody has watched a wave run on any of these ten.
- Eight of the ten have not been balance-tested at all.
- `vs floor` is 1.0× on seven of them: the layouts do not force a detour, so the unmazed route is the
  Manhattan minimum. That matches `crossroads` and is not wrong — the player builds the maze — but
  `comb` at 2.1× is the only one whose geometry does real work.

### What a human should still eyeball

Ten seconds each, on [`level-atlas-iso.png`](../../presentation/docs/level-atlas-iso.png):

1. Can you tell `atoll` from `switchback` at a glance, or do they read as one board in two crops?
2. Does `ringfort` look like a fort, or like a target painted on the floor?
3. On `stepwell`, do the three detached strips on the right read as terraces or as a mistake?
4. `comb` is the hardest map and the most legible one. Is that the level the set should be built around?
5. Is a board with no visible road acceptable, or does the generator need to emit `PathOnly`?
